title: Nominee vs Legal Heir: Who Gets Your Investments Without a Will?

faq.q: What is the primary difference between a nominee and a legal heir?
faq.a: A nominee is a person designated to receive assets from a financial institution upon the account holder's death, primarily to simplify the transfer process. A legal heir is the person legally entitled to inherit the deceased's property according to the applicable laws of succession.

faq.q: Does a nominee always become the owner of the assets?
faq.a: No, not always. For many financial products like bank FDs and mutual funds, the nominee acts as a trustee, holding the assets on behalf of the legal heirs. For some products like PPF, the nominee might become the beneficial owner, especially in the absence of a Will.

faq.q: What happens if I don't name a nominee?
faq.a: If there is no nominee, the legal heirs would need to go through a more complex process to claim the assets, typically involving obtaining a succession certificate or letters of administration from a court, which can be time-consuming and expensive.

faq.q: Can a Will override a nomination?
faq.a: Yes, a valid and properly executed Will generally overrides any nominations made for financial assets. The Will explicitly states your wishes for asset distribution, which takes precedence over the nomination facility.

faq.q: What if my nominee is a minor?
faq.a: If your nominee is a minor, you must appoint an appointee (often a guardian) who will receive the funds on behalf of the minor until they attain majority. Once the minor becomes an adult, they will become the beneficial owner if they are also the legal heir.

faq.q: How do I change my nominee?
faq.a: The process to change a nominee typically involves submitting a nomination change form to the respective financial institution (bank, mutual fund house, etc.). You will need to provide details of the new nominee and often a witness signature.
